## 18.4 Scalar UDF: convenience API

### Array-local implementation

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use arrow_array::{ArrayRef, Int64Array};
use datafusion_common::{cast::as_int64_array, Result};
use datafusion_expr::ColumnarValue;

pub fn add_one(args: &[ColumnarValue]) -> Result<ColumnarValue> {
    if args.len() != 1 {
        return plan_err!("add_one expects exactly one argument");
    }

    let arrays = ColumnarValue::values_to_arrays(args)?;
    let input = as_int64_array(&arrays[0])?;

    let out: Int64Array = input
        .iter()
        .map(|v| v.map(|x| x + 1))
        .collect();

    Ok(ColumnarValue::from(Arc::new(out) as ArrayRef))
}
```

`ColumnarValue` allows a scalar function to receive either arrays or scalars; `ColumnarValue::values_to_arrays` expands scalar values to arrays so a single vectorized path can be used. The convenience scalar UDF API accepts a function of `&[ColumnarValue] -> Result<ColumnarValue>`. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

### Register

```rust
use datafusion_expr::{create_udf, Volatility};
use arrow_schema::DataType;

let add_one_udf = create_udf(
    "add_one",
    vec![DataType::Int64],
    DataType::Int64,
    Volatility::Immutable,
    Arc::new(add_one),
);

let ctx = SessionContext::new();
ctx.register_udf(add_one_udf);
```

`create_udf(name, input_types, return_type, volatility, fun)` is a convenience method for scalar UDFs with a fixed signature and return type; it does not expose advanced features such as input-dependent return types, multiple signatures, or aliases. `SessionContext::register_udf` registers the function under its SQL name, and unquoted SQL function names are looked up lowercase. ([Docs.rs][4])

### Use

```rust
let df = ctx.sql("SELECT add_one(41) AS answer").await?;
df.show().await?;
```

---

## 18.5 Scalar UDF: full `ScalarUDFImpl`

Use `ScalarUDFImpl` when the UDF needs type-dependent return fields, aliases, function documentation, nullability rules, argument coercion, simplification, constraint propagation, output-ordering metadata, or multiple signatures. Required methods are `name`, `signature`, `return_type`, and `invoke_with_args`; provided hooks include `aliases`, `return_field_from_args`, `is_nullable`, `simplify`, `coerce_types`, and others. In DataFusion 54 the trait is `ScalarUDFImpl: Debug + DynEq + DynHash + Send + Sync + Any` — the former required `as_any` method was removed via the `Any` supertrait, and implementations can be recovered with `udf.downcast_ref::<MyImpl>()` on the `ScalarUDF` wrapper. ([Docs.rs][5])

```rust
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct AddOneImpl {
    signature: Signature,
}

impl AddOneImpl {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            signature: Signature::uniform(
                1,
                vec![DataType::Int64],
                Volatility::Immutable,
            ),
        }
    }
}

impl ScalarUDFImpl for AddOneImpl {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "add_one_full"
    }

    fn signature(&self) -> &Signature {
        &self.signature
    }

    fn return_type(&self, arg_types: &[DataType]) -> Result<DataType> {
        if arg_types != [DataType::Int64] {
            return plan_err!("add_one_full expects Int64");
        }
        Ok(DataType::Int64)
    }

    fn invoke_with_args(&self, args: ScalarFunctionArgs) -> Result<ColumnarValue> {
        add_one(&args.args)
    }

    fn is_nullable(&self, _args: &[Expr], _schema: &dyn datafusion_expr::ExprSchema) -> bool {
        true
    }
}

let udf = ScalarUDF::from(AddOneImpl::new());
ctx.register_udf(udf);
```

### Full-implementation rules

```text
Use ScalarUDFImpl when:
  return type depends on input type
  Field metadata / extension metadata must be preserved
  aliases required
  named arguments required
  custom simplification or coercion required
  nullability can be narrower than generic nullable
  function docs should appear in catalogs / help surfaces

Avoid ScalarUDFImpl when:
  fixed input/output types
  simple array transform
  no metadata/simplification/coercion hooks needed
```

---

## 18.6 Named arguments

```rust
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct PowerFunction {
    signature: Signature,
}

impl PowerFunction {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            signature: Signature::uniform(
                2,
                vec![DataType::Float64],
                Volatility::Immutable,
            )
            .with_parameter_names(vec![
                "base".to_string(),
                "exponent".to_string(),
            ])
            .expect("valid parameter names"),
        }
    }
}
```

```sql
SELECT power(base => 2.0, exponent => 8.0);
SELECT power(2.0, exponent => 8.0);
```

DataFusion supports named arguments for scalar, window, and aggregate UDFs, with positional arguments required to appear before named arguments; custom UDF implementations enable named arguments by attaching parameter names to their `Signature` with `.with_parameter_names(...)`. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 18.7 Volatility contract

```text
Volatility::Immutable:
  same output for same inputs forever
  optimizer may constant-fold / simplify aggressively

Volatility::Stable:
  same output for same inputs within one query
  time/session/config-like functions

Volatility::Volatile:
  output may differ for same inputs
  random(), UUID generation, external mutable state
```

The UDF docs describe volatility as an optimization contract: immutable functions always return the same result for the same input, while random-number-like functions are volatile. Incorrect volatility declarations can produce wrong query results after constant folding or expression reuse. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

---

## 18.8 Async scalar UDF

```rust
use datafusion::logical_expr::async_udf::AsyncScalarUDF;

let async_upper = AsyncUpper::new();
let udf = AsyncScalarUDF::new(Arc::new(async_upper));

ctx.register_udf(udf.into_scalar_udf());
```

Async scalar UDFs are for scalar functions that perform async operations such as network or IO calls; they are implemented as async UDFs, converted with `into_scalar_udf`, and then registered like normal scalar UDFs. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

### Async scalar UDF deployment rules

```text
Do:
  bound concurrency
  cache remote lookups where semantically valid
  batch remote calls if possible
  set Volatility correctly
  implement timeout / retry / cancellation policy
  avoid blocking HTTP/file IO inside sync UDF

Do not:
  call blocking clients from scalar UDF hot path
  spawn unbounded tasks per row
  mark external mutable lookups Immutable
```

---

## 18.9 UDAF: accumulator model

```text
Accumulator:
  one accumulator instance = one group state
  update_batch(values)       input batch -> state
  state()                    state -> ScalarValue vector for shuffle/merge
  merge_batch(states)        partial states -> merged state
  evaluate()                 state -> final ScalarValue
  size()                     memory accounting estimate
  retract_batch(values)      optional window-aggregate support
```

DataFusion UDAFs use `Accumulator`, a stateful object representing a single group. Required methods include `update_batch`, `evaluate`, `state`, `merge_batch`, and `size`; the accumulator state is serialized as `ScalarValue`s for efficient multi-phase aggregation, and `GroupsAccumulator` exists as a more complex but higher-performance multi-group API. ([Docs.rs][6])

### Geometric mean UDAF skeleton

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
struct GeometricMean {
    product: f64,
    n: u64,
}

impl GeometricMean {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            product: 1.0,
            n: 0,
        }
    }
}

impl Accumulator for GeometricMean {
    fn update_batch(&mut self, values: &[ArrayRef]) -> Result<()> {
        if values.is_empty() {
            return Ok(());
        }

        let arr = as_float64_array(&values[0])?;

        for v in arr.iter().flatten() {
            self.product *= v;
            self.n += 1;
        }

        Ok(())
    }

    fn merge_batch(&mut self, states: &[ArrayRef]) -> Result<()> {
        if states.len() != 2 {
            return plan_err!("geo_mean merge expects product and count states");
        }

        let products = as_float64_array(&states[0])?;
        let counts = datafusion_common::cast::as_uint64_array(&states[1])?;

        for i in 0..products.len() {
            if let (Some(p), Some(n)) = (products.value(i).into(), counts.value(i).into()) {
                self.product *= p;
                self.n += n;
            }
        }

        Ok(())
    }

    fn state(&mut self) -> Result<Vec<ScalarValue>> {
        Ok(vec![
            ScalarValue::Float64(Some(self.product)),
            ScalarValue::UInt64(Some(self.n)),
        ])
    }

    fn evaluate(&mut self) -> Result<ScalarValue> {
        if self.n == 0 {
            return Ok(ScalarValue::Float64(None));
        }

        Ok(ScalarValue::Float64(Some(
            self.product.powf(1.0 / self.n as f64),
        )))
    }

    fn size(&self) -> usize {
        std::mem::size_of_val(self)
    }
}
```

### Register UDAF

```rust
let geo_mean = create_udaf(
    "geo_mean",
    vec![DataType::Float64],
    Arc::new(DataType::Float64),
    Volatility::Immutable,
    Arc::new(|_args| Ok(Box::new(GeometricMean::new()) as Box<dyn Accumulator>)),
    Arc::new(vec![DataType::Float64, DataType::UInt64]),
);

ctx.register_udaf(geo_mean);
```

`create_udaf` accepts function name, input types, return type, volatility, an accumulator factory, and a state-type description; `SessionContext::register_udaf` registers the aggregate for SQL usage. ([Docs.rs][7])

### Use

```sql
SELECT geo_mean(speed) AS gm
FROM cars;
```

---

## 18.10 UDAF rules

```text
Correctness:
  state_type must match state()
  merge_batch must merge state arrays produced by state()
  evaluate must handle empty/all-null group
  update_batch must ignore nulls unless domain says otherwise
  size must approximate owned state memory

Performance:
  prefer batch iteration over ScalarValue per row where possible
  implement GroupsAccumulator for high-cardinality group-heavy UDAFs
  keep state compact
  avoid heap allocation per row
  support retract_batch only when window aggregate semantics require it

Planner:
  volatility must be correct
  input type signatures must be explicit
  aliases/named args require advanced API
```

---

## 18.11 Window UDF / UDWF

A window UDF takes rows and returns one value per input row while having access to surrounding rows in a partition/window frame. DataFusion’s simple API uses `create_udwf(name, input_type, return_type, volatility, partition_evaluator_factory)`, and the lower-level implementation uses a `PartitionEvaluator`. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

### Partition evaluator skeleton

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
struct MovingAverageEvaluator;

impl PartitionEvaluator for MovingAverageEvaluator {
    fn uses_window_frame(&self) -> bool {
        true
    }

    fn evaluate(
        &mut self,
        values: &[ArrayRef],
        range: &std::ops::Range<usize>,
    ) -> Result<ScalarValue> {
        let arr = as_float64_array(&values[0])?;

        let mut sum = 0.0;
        let mut n = 0usize;

        for i in range.clone() {
            if let Some(v) = arr.value(i).into() {
                sum += v;
                n += 1;
            }
        }

        if n == 0 {
            Ok(ScalarValue::Float64(None))
        } else {
            Ok(ScalarValue::Float64(Some(sum / n as f64)))
        }
    }
}

fn make_partition_evaluator() -> Result<Box<dyn PartitionEvaluator>> {
    Ok(Box::new(MovingAverageEvaluator))
}
```

### Register window UDF

```rust
let smooth_it = create_udwf(
    "smooth_it",
    DataType::Float64,
    Arc::new(DataType::Float64),
    Volatility::Immutable,
    Arc::new(make_partition_evaluator),
);

ctx.register_udwf(smooth_it);
```

### Use

```sql
SELECT
  car,
  speed,
  smooth_it(speed) OVER (
    PARTITION BY car
    ORDER BY time
    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS smooth_speed
FROM cars;
```

The UDF guide notes that `evaluate` is the simplest but slowest window-evaluation API because it is called once per input row, and recommends implementing more advanced methods such as `evaluate_all` or rank-aware variants where possible. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

### Window UDF rules

```text
Use Window UDF when:
  one output row per input row
  function depends on window frame
  SQL OVER semantics required
  grouping aggregate is insufficient

Avoid Window UDF when:
  output row count changes
  scalar UDF is enough
  normal built-in window function exists

Performance:
  implement evaluate_all / batch-oriented API when possible
  avoid O(n^2) frame scans for large partitions
  exploit sorted partition assumptions
  handle empty frames and nulls explicitly
```

---

## 18.12 UDTF / table function

A UDTF takes parameters and returns an `Arc<dyn TableProvider>` for use in a query plan. `TableFunctionImpl::call_with_args` receives `TableFunctionArgs`, reads the argument `Expr`s, validates them, and returns a table provider such as `MemTable` or a custom provider. In DataFusion 54 the trait is `TableFunctionImpl: Debug + Sync + Send + Any` (datafusion-catalog `table.rs`): the legacy `call(&[Expr])` method is deprecated and default-bodied (it errors unless overridden), so implement `call_with_args`, which also exposes the calling session via `args.session()` for config- or catalog-aware providers; the `Any` supertrait enables downcasting registered implementations. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

### Simple `echo(1)` UDTF

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct EchoFunction;

impl TableFunctionImpl for EchoFunction {
    fn call_with_args(&self, args: TableFunctionArgs) -> Result<Arc<dyn TableProvider>> {
        let exprs = args.exprs();

        let Some(Expr::Literal(ScalarValue::Int64(Some(value)), _)) = exprs.get(0) else {
            return plan_err!("echo expects first argument to be Int64 literal");
        };

        if exprs.len() != 1 {
            return plan_err!("echo expects exactly one argument");
        }

        let schema = Arc::new(Schema::new(vec![
            Field::new("a", DataType::Int64, false),
        ]));

        let batch = RecordBatch::try_new(
            schema.clone(),
            vec![Arc::new(Int64Array::from(vec![*value])) as ArrayRef],
        )?;

        let provider = MemTable::try_new(schema, vec![vec![batch]])?;

        Ok(Arc::new(provider))
    }
}

ctx.register_udtf("echo", Arc::new(EchoFunction));
```

### Use

```sql
SELECT * FROM echo(1);
```

`SessionContext::register_udtf(name, fun)` registers a table UDF. DataFusion’s UDTF guide demonstrates an `echo` table function returning a `MemTable` and using it as `SELECT * FROM echo(1)`. ([Docs.rs][8])

### UDTF rules

```text
Use UDTF when:
  table depends on literal/function arguments
  external source should be invoked from FROM clause
  metadata inspection table needed
  interactive table-valued helper needed

Use TableProvider instead when:
  table has stable name/catalog identity
  schema/statistics/capabilities should be registered once
  source should support repeated queries/pushdown

UDTF planning rule:
  call_with_args runs during planning
  keep it cheap
  return provider/plan description, not full remote data where possible
```

---

## 18.13 Custom `TableProvider`

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyProvider {
    schema: SchemaRef,
}

#[async_trait::async_trait]
impl TableProvider for MyProvider {
    fn schema(&self) -> SchemaRef {
        self.schema.clone()
    }

    fn table_type(&self) -> datafusion_expr::TableType {
        datafusion_expr::TableType::Base
    }

    async fn scan(
        &self,
        state: &dyn datafusion::catalog::Session,
        projection: Option<&Vec<usize>>,
        filters: &[Expr],
        limit: Option<usize>,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        // Return custom ExecutionPlan or wrap built-in plan.
        // Keep planning cheap.
        todo!()
    }
}
```

A `TableProvider` is the planning-time abstraction for tables; `scan()` runs during planning, should return quickly, and should describe how the data will be produced rather than performing heavy IO or computation. Built-in examples include `MemTable`, stream tables, `ListingTable`, and `ViewTable`. In DataFusion 54 the trait is `TableProvider: Any + Debug + Sync + Send` (datafusion-catalog `table.rs`); the former required `as_any` method was removed via the `Any` supertrait, and providers are recovered with `downcast_ref::<MyProvider>()` via trait upcasting. ([Apache DataFusion][9])

### Provider rules

```text
scan() should:
  use projection
  use filters where possible
  use limit where possible
  expose partitioning/order/statistics through ExecutionPlan
  stay cheap

scan() should not:
  fetch all data
  block on large remote calls
  collect Vec<RecordBatch>
  open per-query expensive connections unless unavoidable
```

---

## 18.14 Custom physical execution node

### Skeleton

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyExec {
    schema: SchemaRef,
    properties: Arc<PlanProperties>,
}

impl ExecutionPlan for MyExec {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "MyExec"
    }

    fn properties(&self) -> &Arc<PlanProperties> {
        &self.properties
    }

    fn children(&self) -> Vec<&Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        vec![]
    }

    fn with_new_children(
        self: Arc<Self>,
        children: Vec<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>>,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        if !children.is_empty() {
            return plan_err!("MyExec is a leaf plan");
        }
        Ok(self)
    }

    fn execute(
        &self,
        partition: usize,
        context: Arc<datafusion::execution::TaskContext>,
    ) -> Result<SendableRecordBatchStream> {
        // Return custom RecordBatchStream.
        todo!()
    }
}
```

`ExecutionPlan` nodes represent physical plan operators. Required methods include `name`, `properties`, `children`, `with_new_children`, and `execute`; calling `execute` produces an async `SendableRecordBatchStream` of `RecordBatch` values for one partition. Execution-plan properties such as partitioning and ordering communicate physical information to the optimizer. DataFusion 54 removed the required `as_any` method — `Any` is now a supertrait, and optimizer rules downcast with `plan.downcast_ref::<MyExec>()` directly. ([Docs.rs][10])

### Physical node rules

```text
Use custom ExecutionPlan when:
  operator changes row count
  operator requires runtime behavior not expressible with built-ins
  source has custom partitioning/order/pushdown
  specialized IO or index scan needed

Avoid custom ExecutionPlan when:
  scalar UDF is enough
  projection/filter/aggregate/join built-ins suffice
  SQL rewrite to existing operators is possible

Execution:
  never block in poll_next
  expose correct PlanProperties
  support metrics
  respect memory reservations where needed
  keep batch sizes reasonable
```

---

## 18.15 Custom logical node

DataFusion’s `LogicalPlan` enum includes an `Extension` variant for custom logical operators, and `UserDefinedLogicalNodeCore` is the recommended trait for implementing custom logical nodes. Required methods include `name`, `inputs`, `schema`, `expressions`, `fmt_for_explain`, and `with_exprs_and_inputs`; provided hooks control invariant checks, predicate-pushdown barriers, projection pushdown, and limit pushdown. ([Apache DataFusion][11])

```rust
#[derive(Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
struct TopKNode {
    input: LogicalPlan,
    k: usize,
    schema: datafusion_common::DFSchemaRef,
}

impl Debug for TopKNode {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "TopKNode {{ k: {} }}", self.k)
    }
}

impl datafusion_expr::UserDefinedLogicalNodeCore for TopKNode {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "TopK"
    }

    fn inputs(&self) -> Vec<&LogicalPlan> {
        vec![&self.input]
    }

    fn schema(&self) -> &datafusion_common::DFSchemaRef {
        &self.schema
    }

    fn expressions(&self) -> Vec<Expr> {
        vec![]
    }

    fn fmt_for_explain(&self, f: &mut Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "TopK: k={}", self.k)
    }

    fn with_exprs_and_inputs(
        &self,
        _exprs: Vec<Expr>,
        mut inputs: Vec<LogicalPlan>,
    ) -> Result<Self> {
        if inputs.len() != 1 {
            return plan_err!("TopK expects exactly one input");
        }

        Ok(Self {
            input: inputs.remove(0),
            k: self.k,
            schema: self.schema.clone(),
        })
    }

    fn supports_limit_pushdown(&self) -> bool {
        true
    }
}
```

### Logical node rules

```text
Use custom logical node when:
  operation is relational
  optimizer must see it as operator
  DataFrame/SQL needs custom semantic node
  physical behavior requires custom planning

Avoid custom logical node when:
  expression UDF is enough
  SQL can rewrite to built-in operators
  TableProvider + normal scan covers it

Always implement:
  stable schema
  correct expressions()
  correct inputs()
  with_exprs_and_inputs()
  explain formatting
  predicate/projection/limit pushdown semantics
```

---

## 18.16 Logical node → physical node planning

```text
Custom SQL/FROM construct:
  RelationPlanner / ExprPlanner
    -> LogicalPlan::Extension(UserDefinedLogicalNode)

Physical planning:
  ExtensionPlanner / custom QueryPlanner
    -> Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>
```

For SQL constructs that need runtime behavior, such as `TABLESAMPLE`, DataFusion’s extensibility workflow is to parse/plan into a custom logical node, wrap it as `LogicalPlan::Extension`, and then use an extension planner to convert it to a custom `ExecutionPlan`. DataFusion guidance says to prefer rewriting to existing operators when possible and add custom physical operators only when runtime behavior such as randomness or specialized IO requires it. ([Apache DataFusion][12])

---

## 18.17 Custom optimizer rules

### Logical optimizer rule

```rust
use datafusion_common::tree_node::Transformed;
use datafusion_optimizer::optimizer::{OptimizerConfig, OptimizerRule};

#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyRewrite;

impl OptimizerRule for MyRewrite {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "my_rewrite"
    }

    fn rewrite(
        &self,
        plan: LogicalPlan,
        _config: &dyn OptimizerConfig,
    ) -> Result<Transformed<LogicalPlan>> {
        // Return Transformed::yes(new_plan) if rewritten.
        // Return Transformed::no(plan) otherwise.
        Ok(Transformed::no(plan))
    }
}

ctx.add_optimizer_rule(Arc::new(MyRewrite));
```

`SessionContext::add_optimizer_rule` appends a logical optimizer rule to the existing rules. DataFusion’s operator-extension guide demonstrates logical-plan rewriting with an `OptimizerRule::rewrite` implementation that returns either `Transformed::yes(rewritten)` or `Transformed::no(plan)`. ([Docs.rs][8])

### Physical optimizer rule

```rust
use datafusion::physical_optimizer::PhysicalOptimizerRule;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyPhysicalRewrite;

impl PhysicalOptimizerRule for MyPhysicalRewrite {
    fn name(&self) -> &str {
        "my_physical_rewrite"
    }

    fn optimize(
        &self,
        plan: Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>,
        config: &datafusion_common::config::ConfigOptions,
    ) -> Result<Arc<dyn ExecutionPlan>> {
        Ok(plan)
    }

    fn schema_check(&self) -> bool {
        true
    }
}
```

### Rule rules

```text
AnalyzerRule:
  semantic normalization
  may change unresolved forms into valid plan forms

OptimizerRule:
  logical plan
  semantics-preserving
  no data IO

PhysicalOptimizerRule:
  physical plan
  semantics-preserving
  may use partitioning/order/statistics
  no blocking data IO

Custom rules must:
  be deterministic
  preserve schema unless explicitly documented
  preserve query semantics
  have EXPLAIN-based regression tests
```

## 18.18 Custom SQL syntax

### `ExprPlanner`

```rust
use datafusion::sql::planner::{
    PlannerResult, RawBinaryExpr,
};
use datafusion_expr::planner::ExprPlanner;
use datafusion_expr::{BinaryExpr, Operator};
use sqlparser::ast::BinaryOperator;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyCustomPlanner;

impl ExprPlanner for MyCustomPlanner {
    fn plan_binary_op(
        &self,
        expr: RawBinaryExpr,
        _schema: &datafusion_common::DFSchema,
    ) -> Result<PlannerResult<RawBinaryExpr>> {
        match &expr.op {
            BinaryOperator::Arrow => {
                Ok(PlannerResult::Planned(Expr::BinaryExpr(BinaryExpr {
                    left: Box::new(expr.left.clone()),
                    op: Operator::StringConcat,
                    right: Box::new(expr.right.clone()),
                })))
            }
            _ => Ok(PlannerResult::Original(expr)),
        }
    }
}

let config = SessionConfig::new()
    .set_str("datafusion.sql_parser.dialect", "postgres");

let mut ctx = SessionContext::new_with_config(config);
ctx.register_expr_planner(Arc::new(MyCustomPlanner))?;
```

DataFusion provides custom expression planning for SQL syntax that is parsed but not natively planned, such as custom binary operators; `ExprPlanner` can map raw SQL AST expression forms into logical `Expr`, and `SessionContext` exposes registration through the function-registry interface. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

### SQL extension decision tree

```text
Custom scalar expression:
  ExprPlanner -> existing Expr / ScalarUDF

Custom type syntax:
  TypePlanner

Custom FROM/table factor:
  RelationPlanner -> existing LogicalPlan or LogicalPlan::Extension

Runtime-only relation behavior:
  RelationPlanner -> custom logical node -> ExtensionPlanner -> custom ExecutionPlan

Statement-level syntax:
  parser wrapper or upstream contribution may be required
```

DataFusion’s SQL extensibility guidance recommends an incremental workflow: parse with a wrapper if needed, plan with `ExprPlanner`, `TypePlanner`, or `RelationPlanner`, and prefer rewrites to existing operators before adding custom physical operators via an extension planner. ([Apache DataFusion][12])

---

## 18.19 Registration matrix

| Artifact           | Register with                                             |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Scalar UDF         | `ctx.register_udf(ScalarUDF)`                             |
| Async scalar UDF   | `ctx.register_udf(async_udf.into_scalar_udf())`           |
| Aggregate UDF      | `ctx.register_udaf(AggregateUDF)`                         |
| Window UDF         | `ctx.register_udwf(WindowUDF)`                            |
| Table UDF          | `ctx.register_udtf("name", Arc<dyn TableFunctionImpl>)`   |
| TableProvider      | `ctx.register_table("name", Arc<dyn TableProvider>)`      |
| Object store       | `ctx.register_object_store(url, Arc<dyn ObjectStore>)`    |
| Analyzer rule      | `ctx.add_analyzer_rule(Arc<dyn AnalyzerRule>)`            |
| Optimizer rule     | `ctx.add_optimizer_rule(Arc<dyn OptimizerRule>)`          |
| Expr planner       | `ctx.register_expr_planner(Arc<dyn ExprPlanner>)`         |
| Relation planner   | `ctx.register_relation_planner(Arc<dyn RelationPlanner>)` |
| Physical optimizer | `SessionStateBuilder::with_physical_optimizer_rule(...)`  |
| Query planner      | `SessionStateBuilder::with_query_planner(...)`            |

`SessionContext` exposes registration methods for UDFs, UDAFs, UDWFs, UDTFs, tables, object stores, analyzer rules, optimizer rules, expression planners, and relation planners; builder-level `SessionStateBuilder` APIs provide tighter control over rule order and physical/query planner composition. ([Docs.rs][8])

## 18.20 Testing scalar UDFs against Arrow arrays

### Direct array-level test

```rust
#[test]
fn add_one_direct_array_test() -> Result<()> {
    let input = ColumnarValue::from(
        Arc::new(Int64Array::from(vec![Some(1), None, Some(3)])) as ArrayRef
    );

    let result = add_one(&[input])?;
    let array = result.into_array(3)?;

    let output = as_int64_array(&array)?;
    assert_eq!(output, &Int64Array::from(vec![Some(2), None, Some(4)]));

    Ok(())
}
```

The UDF guide explicitly recommends testing the function implementation in isolation with `ColumnarValue` and Arrow arrays before registering it with DataFusion. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

### SQL registration test

```rust
#[tokio::test]
async fn add_one_sql_test() -> Result<()> {
    let ctx = SessionContext::new();

    ctx.register_udf(create_udf(
        "add_one",
        vec![DataType::Int64],
        DataType::Int64,
        Volatility::Immutable,
        Arc::new(add_one),
    ));

    let df = ctx.sql("SELECT add_one(1) AS v").await?;
    let batches = df.collect().await?;

    datafusion::assert_batches_eq!(
        &[
            "+---+",
            "| v |",
            "+---+",
            "| 2 |",
            "+---+",
        ],
        &batches
    );

    Ok(())
}
```

## 18.21 Testing UDAFs

```rust
#[test]
fn geo_mean_accumulator_direct_test() -> Result<()> {
    let input: ArrayRef = Arc::new(Float64Array::from(vec![
        Some(2.0),
        Some(8.0),
    ]));

    let mut acc = GeometricMean::new();
    acc.update_batch(&[input])?;

    assert_eq!(
        acc.evaluate()?,
        ScalarValue::Float64(Some(4.0))
    );

    let state = acc.state()?;
    assert_eq!(state.len(), 2);

    Ok(())
}
```

```rust
#[tokio::test]
async fn geo_mean_sql_test() -> Result<()> {

    );
```

```rust
#[tokio::test]
async fn custom_arrow_operator_test() -> Result<()> {
    let config = SessionConfig::new()
        .set_str("datafusion.sql_parser.dialect", "postgres");

    let mut ctx = SessionContext::new_with_config(config);
    ctx.register_expr_planner(Arc::new(MyCustomPlanner))?;

    );

    Ok(())
```

The DataFusion UDF guide includes this `ExprPlanner` pattern for the `->` binary operator and uses `assert_batches_eq!` to verify the planned expression produces `foobar`. ([Apache DataFusion][3])

## 18.24 Performance and safety rules

```text
Scalar UDF:
  vectorize over Arrow arrays
  preserve row count
  avoid per-row allocation
  handle Scalar and Array ColumnarValue
  define null behavior explicitly

Async UDF:
  no blocking IO
  bounded concurrency
  timeout/retry policy
  correct volatility

UDAF:
  compact state
  correct state_type
  batch update/merge
  empty/all-null behavior
  memory size estimate

Window UDF:
  avoid per-row frame scans when possible
  implement batch/rank-aware methods where possible
  test partition/frame/null behavior

UDTF:
  keep planning cheap
  return TableProvider
  validate literal/non-literal args
  avoid fetching full external data during planning

TableProvider:
  push projection/filter/limit
  expose statistics/partitioning/order
  keep scan cheap

ExecutionPlan:
  stream batches
  do not block in poll_next
  expose correct PlanProperties
  implement metrics/memory discipline

SQL extension:
  rewrite to existing Expr/LogicalPlan when possible
  add custom physical operator only for required runtime behavior
```

---

## 18.25 Anti-pattern catalog

| Anti-pattern                                            | Failure mode                       | Correct pattern                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| scalar UDF returns different row count                  | execution error / wrong semantics  | UDTF or custom `ExecutionPlan`          |
| scalar UDF expands all scalars blindly                  | unnecessary allocation             | scalar-specialized fast path            |
| blocking HTTP call inside scalar UDF                    | runtime starvation                 | async scalar UDF                        |
| UDAF state type mismatches `state()`                    | merge failure / wrong results      | explicit state test                     |
| UDAF ignores all-null group                             | wrong SQL semantics                | return typed null where appropriate     |
| window UDF uses `evaluate` O(n²) for large partitions   | poor performance                   | `evaluate_all` style implementation     |
| UDTF fetches remote table during planning               | slow planning / deadlocks          | return provider, fetch during execution |
| custom TableProvider reads all data in `scan`           | lost pushdown and planning latency | return `ExecutionPlan`                  |
| custom logical node omits expressions                   | optimizer cannot rewrite           | implement `expressions()` correctly     |
| optimizer rule changes result semantics                 | wrong answers                      | analyzer or explicit custom operator    |
| custom SQL parser fork for simple operator              | maintenance burden                 | `ExprPlanner`                           |
| physical operator with wrong partition/order properties | optimizer mis-plans                | correct `PlanProperties` tests          |

---

## 18.26 Golden test matrix

```text
Scalar UDF:
  direct ColumnarValue::Array
  direct ColumnarValue::Scalar
  null input
  all-null input
  wrong arity
  wrong type
  SQL registration
  DataFrame expression invocation
  named arguments if supported
  volatility constant-fold behavior if critical

Async scalar UDF:
  timeout
  cancellation
  bounded concurrency
  error mapping
  volatility behavior

UDAF:
  direct accumulator update/evaluate
  state/merge round trip
  empty input
  all-null input
  grouped aggregate
  multi-partition aggregate
  wrong state type negative test
  memory size nonzero

Window UDF:
  partition boundary
  frame boundary
  empty frame
  null values
  ORDER BY behavior
  large partition performance
  SQL OVER invocation

UDTF:
  literal args
  invalid args
  returned schema
  SQL FROM invocation
  projection/filter interaction if provider supports it

TableProvider:
  scan projection
  filter pushdown
  limit pushdown
  partitioning
  statistics
  EXPLAIN plan shape
  no heavy IO in scan

Custom logical node:
  schema
  inputs
  expressions
  with_exprs_and_inputs
  explain text
  predicate pushdown barrier
  projection pushdown behavior
  limit pushdown behavior

Custom physical node:
  execute partition 0
  multiple partitions
  stream error propagation
  batch schema consistency
  PlanProperties
  metrics
  memory/spill behavior if applicable

Optimizer rules:
  no-op path
  rewrite path
  semantic equivalence
  rule ordering
  EXPLAIN snapshots

Custom SQL syntax:
  parser dialect
  ExprPlanner fallback Original
  planned custom operator
  unsupported syntax error
  nested query / CTE behavior if relevant
```

---

## 18.27 Value case

```text
Scalar UDF:
  value = SQL/DataFrame-visible vectorized domain function.

Async Scalar UDF:
  value = external async lookup/inference/IO inside query plans.

UDAF:
  value = reusable grouped aggregate with distributed partial-merge support.

Window UDF:
  value = custom per-row analytics over SQL partitions and frames.

UDTF:
  value = function-call syntax for dynamic table providers.

TableProvider:
  value = custom data source with projection/filter/limit/statistics integration.

UserDefinedLogicalNode:
  value = optimizer-visible custom relational operator.

ExecutionPlan:
  value = custom runtime behavior and streaming physical operator.

OptimizerRule:
  value = domain-specific plan rewrite and pushdown.

ExprPlanner / TypePlanner / RelationPlanner:
  value = dialect compatibility without full SQL fork.

Testing against Arrow arrays:
  value = fast deterministic validation before involving SQL planner/execution engine.
```

Final agent rule:

```text
Use UDFs for value-producing expressions.
Use UDAFs for grouped stateful reductions.
Use UDWFs for window-frame semantics.
Use UDTFs for function-returned tables.
Use TableProvider for named/custom sources.
Use UserDefinedLogicalNode + ExecutionPlan only for real relational operators.
Use optimizer rules for equivalent rewrites.
Use SQL planners for dialect syntax.
Test the Arrow-array implementation first, then SQL registration, then plan shape.
```

## 18.28 Higher-order UDFs and SQL lambdas (DataFusion 54)

Secondary coverage — the authoring deep dive is `datafusion_calculations_rust.md`. DataFusion 54 adds first-class higher-order functions: functions whose arguments include lambda expressions.

### SQL surface

```sql
SELECT array_transform(xs, x -> x + 1)        FROM t;  -- map
SELECT array_filter(xs, x -> x % 2 = 0)       FROM t;  -- filter
SELECT array_any_match(xs, x -> x > 100)      FROM t;  -- exists
```

These built-ins (datafusion-functions-nested) replace the DF-53-era `UNNEST` → transform → re-`array_agg` pipelines for per-element array work.

### Expression model

Three new `Expr` variants (datafusion-expr `expr.rs`):

```text
Expr::HigherOrderFunction(HigherOrderFunction)  # invocation of a HigherOrderUDF
Expr::Lambda(Lambda)                            # parameter names + body expression
Expr::LambdaVariable(LambdaVariable)            # named reference to a lambda parameter
```

Caveat for expression visitors/rewriters: `LambdaVariable` is **not** a `Column` — column-resolution, schema-lookup, and dependency-analysis passes that assume every leaf name is a column must special-case lambda variables.

### Implementing and registering

```rust
use datafusion_expr::higher_order_function::{HigherOrderUDF, HigherOrderUDFImpl};

// impl trait (Debug + DynEq + DynHash + Send + Sync + Any):
//   fn name(&self) -> &str
//   fn signature(&self) -> &HigherOrderSignature
//   fn lambda_parameters(...) -> Result<LambdaParametersProgress>
//   fn return_field_from_args(...) / invoke hooks
struct MyReduce { /* … */ }

// wrap and register:
let udf = HigherOrderUDF::new_from_impl(MyReduce::new());
ctx.register_higher_order_function(Arc::new(udf));
```

`HigherOrderUDFImpl` is the implementation trait; `HigherOrderUDF` is the registration wrapper (datafusion-expr `higher_order_function.rs`; `array_transform.rs` in datafusion-functions-nested is the commented reference implementation). `FunctionRegistry` gains `register_higher_order_function`, `deregister_higher_order_function`, `higher_order_function(name)`, and `higher_order_function_names()` alongside the scalar/aggregate/window registries in §18.19.

# 19) Flight RPC and Flight SQL

Style target: dense, syntax-first, agent-ready technical reference; aligned with the uploaded advanced-reference format. 

---

## 19.0 Mental model

```text
Arrow Flight RPC:
  Arrow RecordBatch stream transport over gRPC
  metadata discovery via FlightInfo / FlightEndpoint / Ticket
  upload via DoPut
  download via DoGet
  custom service actions via DoAction
  optional auth through handshake / metadata / gRPC middleware

Flight SQL:
  SQL/database protocol layered on Flight RPC
  SQL commands encoded into FlightDescriptor::cmd or Action::body
  query results and metadata returned as Arrow RecordBatch streams
  prepared statements, catalog metadata, updates, ingest, transactions
```

The Rust `arrow-flight` crate contains prost-generated Flight protobuf structs such as `FlightData`, `FlightInfo`, `Location`, and `Ticket`; tonic-generated low-level Flight clients/servers; high-level encoding/decoding helpers for Arrow `RecordBatch` streams; and Flight SQL support behind the `flight-sql` feature. ([Docs.rs][1])

---

## 19.3 Protocol objects

| Object                | Rust type               | Role                                                                  |
| --------------------- | ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| stream payload        | `FlightData`            | IPC-framed Arrow schema/dictionaries/record batches plus app metadata |
| data discovery result | `FlightInfo`            | schema, endpoints, row/byte estimates, descriptor                     |
| endpoint              | `FlightEndpoint`        | ticket + possible locations for a stream fragment                     |
| stream token          | `Ticket`                | opaque server-defined token redeemed by `DoGet`                       |
| service location      | `Location`              | URI where endpoint may be fetched                                     |
| dataset identity      | `FlightDescriptor`      | path descriptor or binary command descriptor                          |
| schema-only result    | `SchemaResult`          | IPC-encoded schema returned by `GetSchema`                            |
| upload result         | `PutResult`             | server result metadata from `DoPut`                                   |
| custom action         | `Action` / `ActionType` | service-specific RPC commands                                         |

The Flight protocol’s normal download flow is: client obtains or constructs a `FlightDescriptor`, calls `GetFlightInfo`, receives `FlightInfo` containing one or more `FlightEndpoint`s, then calls `DoGet(Ticket)` for each endpoint to receive Arrow record batches. If endpoint ordering matters, `FlightInfo.ordered` signals ordered concatenation semantics; otherwise clients may fetch endpoints in arbitrary/interleaved order. ([Apache Arrow][3])

---

## 19.4 Flight service/client basics

### Client construction

```rust
let endpoint = Endpoint::from_static("http://127.0.0.1:50051");
let channel: Channel = endpoint.connect().await?;

let mut client = FlightClient::new(channel);

// Per-request metadata, e.g. bearer token.
client.add_header("authorization", "Bearer <token>")?;
```

`FlightClient::new(channel)` wraps a tonic `Channel`, and `metadata_mut` / `add_header` allow request metadata such as authorization headers or other application-specific gRPC headers to be attached to subsequent requests. ([Docs.rs][4])

### Get schema

```rust
let descriptor = FlightDescriptor::new_cmd(b"SELECT * FROM t".to_vec());

let schema: Schema = client
    .get_schema(descriptor)
    .await?;
```

### Get FlightInfo then fetch tickets

```rust
let descriptor = FlightDescriptor::new_cmd(b"dataset:orders".to_vec());

let info: FlightInfo = client
    .get_flight_info(descriptor)
    .await?;

for endpoint in info.endpoint {
    let Some(ticket) = endpoint.ticket else {
        continue;
    };

    let mut stream = client.do_get(ticket).await?;

    while let Some(batch) = stream.next().await {
        let batch = batch?;
        // process RecordBatch
    }
}
```

High-level `FlightClient` exposes `get_flight_info`, `do_get`, `do_put`, `list_flights`, `get_schema`, `list_actions`, `do_action`, `cancel_flight_info`, and `renew_flight_endpoint`; `do_get` returns a `FlightRecordBatchStream`, while `get_flight_info` returns `FlightInfo`. ([Docs.rs][4])

---

## 19.5 Encoding `RecordBatch` streams to `FlightData`

### Encode stream for `DoGet`

```rust
use futures::stream;

let input = stream::iter(vec![
    Ok(batch_1),
    Ok(batch_2),
]);

let flight_data_stream = FlightDataEncoderBuilder::new()
    .with_schema(schema.clone())
    .with_max_flight_data_size(2 * 1024 * 1024)
    .build(input);

let response = Response::new(flight_data_stream);
```

`FlightDataEncoderBuilder` turns a `Stream<Item = Result<RecordBatch, FlightError>>` into a stream of `FlightData`, which is the normal server-side shape for implementing `DoGet`; it can accept a known schema, app metadata, IPC writer options, dictionary handling policy, and a maximum approximate message size. The default max FlightData target is 2 MiB because gRPC message sizes are commonly bounded. ([Apache Arrow][5])

### Dictionary handling

```rust
let flight_data_stream = FlightDataEncoderBuilder::new()
    .with_schema(schema)
    // choose dictionary handling if required by interop target
    .build(input_stream);
```

Encoding dictionary arrays requires an explicit interoperability decision: hydrate dictionaries into underlying values for broad compatibility, or resend dictionary data with batches when dictionary transport semantics are desired. The encoder docs call out this caveat directly. ([Apache Arrow][5])

---

## 19.6 Decoding `FlightData` to `RecordBatch`

### Client `DoGet` already decodes

```rust
let mut batches: FlightRecordBatchStream = client
    .do_get(ticket)
    .await?;

while let Some(batch) = batches.next().await {
    let batch = batch?;
    // RecordBatch
}
```

### Low-level decode pattern

```rust
let raw_stream = low_level_flight_service_client
    .do_get(Request::new(ticket))
    .await?
    .into_inner();

let mut batch_stream = FlightRecordBatchStream::new_from_flight_data(
    raw_stream.map_err(|status| FlightError::Tonic(Box::new(status))),
);

while let Some(batch) = batch_stream.next().await {
    let batch = batch?;
}
```

`arrow-flight` re-exports a `decode` module for converting `FlightData` streams into `RecordBatch` streams and an `encode` module for converting `RecordBatch` streams into `FlightData` streams. ([Docs.rs][1])

---

## 19.7 Implementing a core Flight server with `tonic`

### Service skeleton

```rust
#[derive(Clone)]
struct MyFlightService {
    schema: SchemaRef,
    batches: Arc<Vec<RecordBatch>>,
}

type BoxFlightStream<T> = Pin<Box<dyn Stream<Item = Result<T, Status>> + Send + 'static>>;

#[tonic::async_trait]
impl FlightService for MyFlightService {
    type HandshakeStream = BoxFlightStream<HandshakeResponse>;
    type ListFlightsStream = BoxFlightStream<FlightInfo>;
    type DoGetStream = Pin<Box<dyn Stream<Item = FlightResult<FlightData>> + Send + 'static>>;
    type DoPutStream = BoxFlightStream<PutResult>;
    type DoActionStream = BoxFlightStream<arrow_flight::Result>;
    type ListActionsStream = BoxFlightStream<ActionType>;
    type DoExchangeStream = Pin<Box<dyn Stream<Item = Result<FlightData, Status>> + Send + 'static>>;

    async fn get_flight_info(
        &self,
        request: Request<FlightDescriptor>,
    ) -> Result<Response<FlightInfo>, Status> {
        let descriptor = request.into_inner();

        let ticket = Ticket {
            ticket: b"orders".to_vec().into(),
        };

        let endpoint = FlightEndpoint {
            ticket: Some(ticket),
            location: vec![],
            expiration_time: None,
            app_metadata: Bytes::new(),
        };

        let info = FlightInfo::new()
            .try_with_schema(self.schema.as_ref())
            .map_err(to_status)?
            .with_endpoint(endpoint)
            .with_descriptor(descriptor)
            .with_ordered(true);

        Ok(Response::new(info))
    }

    async fn do_get(
        &self,
        request: Request<Ticket>,
    ) -> Result<Response<Self::DoGetStream>, Status> {
        let ticket = request.into_inner();

        if ticket.ticket.as_ref() != b"orders" {
            return Err(Status::not_found("unknown ticket"));
        }

        let input = futures::stream::iter(
            self.batches.iter().cloned().map(Ok::<_, FlightError>)
        );

        let output = FlightDataEncoderBuilder::new()
            .with_schema(self.schema.clone())
            .build(input);

        Ok(Response::new(Box::pin(output)))
    }

    async fn list_flights(
        &self,
        _request: Request<Criteria>,
    ) -> Result<Response<Self::ListFlightsStream>, Status> {
        let stream = futures::stream::empty();
        Ok(Response::new(Box::pin(stream)))
    }

    async fn get_schema(
        &self,
        _request: Request<FlightDescriptor>,
    ) -> Result<Response<SchemaResult>, Status> {
        let options = arrow_ipc::writer::IpcWriteOptions::default();
        let schema = arrow_flight::utils::flight_schema_as_encoded_data(
            self.schema.as_ref(),
            &options,
        )
        .map_err(to_status)?;

        Ok(Response::new(SchemaResult {
            schema: schema.data_header,
        }))
    }

    async fn do_put(
        &self,
        _request: Request<tonic::Streaming<FlightData>>,
    ) -> Result<Response<Self::DoPutStream>, Status> {
        Err(Status::unimplemented("do_put not implemented"))
    }

    async fn handshake(
        &self,
        _request: Request<tonic::Streaming<HandshakeRequest>>,
    ) -> Result<Response<Self::HandshakeStream>, Status> {
        Err(Status::unimplemented("handshake not implemented"))
    }

    async fn list_actions(
        &self,
        _request: Request<Empty>,
    ) -> Result<Response<Self::ListActionsStream>, Status> {
        Ok(Response::new(Box::pin(futures::stream::empty())))
    }

    async fn do_action(
        &self,
        _request: Request<Action>,
    ) -> Result<Response<Self::DoActionStream>, Status> {
        Err(Status::unimplemented("action not implemented"))
    }

    async fn do_exchange(
        &self,
        _request: Request<tonic::Streaming<FlightData>>,
    ) -> Result<Response<Self::DoExchangeStream>, Status> {
        Err(Status::unimplemented("do_exchange not implemented"))
    }
}

fn to_status<E: std::fmt::Display>(e: E) -> Status {
    Status::internal(e.to_string())
}
```

### Serve

```rust
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let addr = "0.0.0.0:50051".parse()?;

    let schema = Arc::new(Schema::new(vec![
        Field::new("id", DataType::Int64, false),
        Field::new("name", DataType::Utf8, true),
    ]));

    let batch = RecordBatch::try_from_iter(vec![
        ("id", Arc::new(Int64Array::from(vec![1, 2, 3])) as ArrayRef),
        ("name", Arc::new(StringArray::from(vec!["a", "b", "c"])) as ArrayRef),
    ])?;

    let service = MyFlightService {
        schema,
        batches: Arc::new(vec![batch]),
    };

    Server::builder()
        .add_service(FlightServiceServer::new(service))
        .serve(addr)
        .await?;

    Ok(())
}
```

The low-level generated Flight service/client are tonic services; protocol RPCs include `ListFlights`, `GetFlightInfo`, `DoGet`, `DoPut`, `GetSchema`, `DoAction`, and related methods. ([Docs.rs][6])

---

## 19.8 Flight endpoint / location semantics

```text
FlightInfo:
  descriptor
  schema
  endpoints[]
  total_records estimate
  total_bytes estimate
  ordered flag

FlightEndpoint:
  ticket
  locations[]
  expiration_time
  app_metadata

Location:
  URI to Flight server or external HTTP/HTTPS object
```

If a server returns an empty endpoint `locations` list, the client should reuse the original Flight service connection; otherwise the client should connect to one of the listed locations. Flight also supports extended HTTP/HTTPS locations for direct downloads, where the client should ignore `Ticket` and treat the object as Arrow IPC unless media type says otherwise. ([Apache Arrow][3])

Agent rule:

```text
Single-server deployment:
  endpoint.location = []
  ticket identifies result on same service

Distributed deployment:
  endpoint.location = [grpc://host:port]
  ticket is redeemed at that server

Object-store / presigned URL deployment:
  endpoint.location = [https://...]
  ticket ignored by client
  content type should identify IPC / Parquet / other format
```

---

## 19.9 Uploading with `DoPut`

### Client-side upload

```rust
let descriptor = FlightDescriptor::new_path(vec!["upload".to_string(), "events".to_string()]);

let input_batches = futures::stream::iter(vec![Ok(batch)]);

let flight_data = FlightDataEncoderBuilder::new()
    .with_schema(schema)
    .with_descriptor(descriptor)
    .build(input_batches);

let mut results = client.do_put(flight_data).await?;

while let Some(result) = results.next().await {
    let result: PutResult = result?;
    // result.app_metadata may contain service-specific response
}
```

### Server-side receive

```rust
async fn do_put(
    &self,
    request: Request<tonic::Streaming<FlightData>>,
) -> Result<Response<Self::DoPutStream>, Status> {
    let stream = request.into_inner();

    let mut batches = FlightRecordBatchStream::new_from_flight_data(
        stream.map_err(|status| FlightError::Tonic(Box::new(status))),
    );

    while let Some(batch) = batches.next().await {
        let batch = batch.map_err(to_status)?;
        // persist / validate / ingest
    }

    let output = futures::stream::iter(vec![
        Ok(PutResult {
            app_metadata: Bytes::from_static(b"ok"),
        }),
    ]);

    Ok(Response::new(Box::pin(output)))
}
```

`FlightClient::do_put` accepts a stream of `FlightData` and returns a stream of `PutResult`; the encoder can include a `FlightDescriptor` so the server knows what the uploaded data represents. ([Docs.rs][4])

---

## 19.10 Error mapping

| Flight error intent               | `tonic::Status`             |
| --------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| invalid descriptor / SQL / ticket | `Status::invalid_argument`  |
| unknown ticket / missing stream   | `Status::not_found`         |
| unsupported RPC                   | `Status::unimplemented`     |
| unauthenticated                   | `Status::unauthenticated`   |
| authenticated but forbidden       | `Status::permission_denied` |
| internal execution failure        | `Status::internal`          |
| server overloaded / unavailable   | `Status::unavailable`       |
| cancelled query                   | `Status::cancelled`         |
| deadline exceeded                 | `Status::deadline_exceeded` |

The Arrow Flight specification defines cross-language error codes including `UNKNOWN`, `INTERNAL`, `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, `TIMED_OUT`, `NOT_FOUND`, `ALREADY_EXISTS`, `CANCELLED`, `UNAUTHENTICATED`, `UNAUTHORIZED`, `UNIMPLEMENTED`, and `UNAVAILABLE`; Rust tonic status codes should be selected to preserve those semantics as closely as possible. ([Apache Arrow][3])

---

## 19.11 Flight SQL concepts

```text
Flight SQL:
  SQL command messages are protobuf messages
  command packed into google.protobuf.Any
  serialized into FlightDescriptor::cmd or Action::body
  GetFlightInfo/GetSchema returns metadata about result stream
  DoGet retrieves Arrow data using tickets
  DoPut handles updates / ingest / prepared statement parameter binding
  DoAction handles actions such as prepare, close, begin transaction, end transaction
```

Flight SQL is a protocol for SQL databases over Arrow Flight. SQL metadata commands use `GetFlightInfo` / `GetSchema`, with request messages packed into `FlightDescriptor::cmd`; when the server returns `FlightInfo`, the client uses returned tickets with `DoGet` to retrieve Arrow metadata/result batches. Query execution and prepared-statement management use the same Flight RPC methods plus Flight SQL command/action messages. ([Apache Arrow][7])

---

## 19.12 Flight SQL client

### Connect

```rust
let channel = Endpoint::from_static("http://127.0.0.1:50051")
    .connect()
    .await?;

let inner = FlightServiceClient::new(channel);
let mut client = FlightSqlServiceClient::new(inner);
```

### Execute SQL query

```rust
let info = client
    .execute("SELECT user_id, amount FROM orders".to_string(), None)
    .await?;

for endpoint in info.endpoint {
    let Some(ticket) = endpoint.ticket else {
        continue;
    };

    let mut stream = client
        .inner_mut()
        .do_get(Request::new(ticket))
        .await?
        .into_inner();

    let mut batches = FlightRecordBatchStream::new_from_flight_data(
        stream.map_err(|status| FlightError::Tonic(Box::new(status))),
    );

    while let Some(batch) = batches.next().await {
        let batch = batch?;
    }
}
```

### Metadata APIs

```rust
let catalogs: FlightInfo = client.get_catalogs().await?;
let tables: FlightInfo = client.get_tables(CommandGetTables {
    catalog: None,
    db_schema_filter_pattern: None,
    table_name_filter_pattern: None,
    table_types: vec![],
    include_schema: false,
}).await?;

let info: FlightInfo = client
    .get_sql_info(vec![
        SqlInfo::FlightSqlServerName,
        SqlInfo::FlightSqlServerVersion,
        SqlInfo::FlightSqlServerSql,
    ])
    .await?;
```

`FlightSqlServiceClient` wraps the underlying Flight client and exposes Flight SQL-specific calls such as `get_tables`, `get_primary_keys`, `get_exported_keys`, `get_imported_keys`, `get_cross_reference`, `get_table_types`, `get_sql_info`, `get_xdbc_type_info`, and prepared statement APIs. ([Docs.rs][8])

---

## 19.13 Prepared statements

### Create, inspect, bind, execute, close

```rust
let mut prepared = client
    .prepare(
        "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?".to_string(),
        None, // transaction_id
    )
    .await?;

let parameter_schema = prepared.parameter_schema()?;
let dataset_schema = prepared.dataset_schema()?;

// Parameter batch must match server-provided bind schema.
let params = RecordBatch::try_from_iter(vec![
    ("customer_id", Arc::new(Int64Array::from(vec![42_i64])) as ArrayRef),
])?;

prepared.set_parameters(params)?;

let info = prepared.execute().await?;

// Fetch result tickets from info...
for endpoint in info.endpoint {
    if let Some(ticket) = endpoint.ticket {
        let mut stream = client.inner_mut().do_get(Request::new(ticket)).await?.into_inner();
        // decode FlightData -> RecordBatch
    }
}

prepared.close().await?;
```

`PreparedStatement` exposes `execute`, `execute_update`, `parameter_schema`, `dataset_schema`, `set_parameters(RecordBatch)`, and `close`; the Flight SQL spec warns that schemas returned at prepare time may be absent or may not exactly match execution-time output because result schemas can depend on bound parameters. ([Docs.rs][9])

### Prepared-statement rules

```text
Client:
  always close prepared statements
  treat prepare-time schemas as hints, not final truth
  bind parameters as RecordBatch matching parameter schema
  fetch final data through FlightInfo endpoints

Server:
  handles are opaque
  support stateless handles if desired
  prepared statement parameter binding may use DoPut
  close action must free server resources
```

---

The `FlightSqlService` helper trait is feature-gated by `flight-sql` and provides methods for SQL statements, Substrait plans, prepared statements, metadata APIs, `DoGet`, `DoPut`, `DoAction`, and fallbacks. Most methods have default behavior, while server implementations override the subset they support. ([Apache Arrow][10])

### Flight SQL metadata methods

```text
get_flight_info_catalogs
get_flight_info_schemas
get_flight_info_tables
get_flight_info_table_types
get_flight_info_sql_info
get_flight_info_primary_keys
get_flight_info_exported_keys
get_flight_info_imported_keys
get_flight_info_cross_reference
get_flight_info_xdbc_type_info
```

Flight SQL metadata commands cover catalogs, schemas, table lists, table types, SQL server feature info, primary keys, imported/exported keys, cross references, and XDBC type information; the schemas returned by `GetSchema` or `DoGet` for each metadata command are fixed by the Flight SQL specification. ([Apache Arrow][7])

## 19.15 Transactions and savepoints

Flight SQL defines actions for `BeginTransaction`, `EndTransaction`, `BeginSavepoint`, and `EndSavepoint`, plus server-info flags indicating support for transactions and ingest transactions. These are Flight SQL API-level operations, distinct from SQL text such as `BEGIN` / `COMMIT`; servers should advertise support through `SqlInfo` values and return `UNIMPLEMENTED` / equivalent status for unsupported transaction actions. ([Docs.rs][11])

```text
Transaction action flow:
  client DoAction(BeginTransaction)
  server returns transaction_id bytes
  client includes transaction_id in execute / prepare / update calls
  client DoAction(EndTransaction commit=true|false)

Savepoint action flow:
  BeginSavepoint(transaction_id, name?)
  EndSavepoint(transaction_id, savepoint_id, action)
```

Agent rules:

```text
If backend is DataFusion-only:
  transaction support may be application-defined
  do not advertise full transactional semantics unless storage layer supports them

If backend is database engine:
  map transaction_id to backend transaction/session
  enforce timeout and cleanup
  close/rollback abandoned transactions
```

---

## 19.16 TLS, auth, and middleware

### TLS server

```rust
use tonic::transport::{Identity, Server, ServerTlsConfig};

let cert = std::fs::read("server.pem")?;
let key = std::fs::read("server.key")?;

let identity = Identity::from_pem(cert, key);

Server::builder()
    .tls_config(ServerTlsConfig::new().identity(identity))?
    .add_service(FlightServiceServer::new(service))
    .serve(addr)
    .await?;
```

### TLS client

```rust
use tonic::transport::{Certificate, ClientTlsConfig, Endpoint};

let ca = std::fs::read("ca.pem")?;
let tls = ClientTlsConfig::new()
    .ca_certificate(Certificate::from_pem(ca))
    .domain_name("flight.example.com");

let channel = Endpoint::from_static("https://flight.example.com:443")
    .tls_config(tls)?
    .connect()
    .await?;
```

### Header auth

```rust
client.add_header("authorization", "Bearer <token>")?;
```

### Server interceptor sketch

```rust
use tonic::service::Interceptor;
use tonic::{Request, Status};

#[derive(Clone)]
struct AuthInterceptor;

impl Interceptor for AuthInterceptor {
    fn call(&mut self, req: Request<()>) -> Result<Request<()>, Status> {
        let ok = req
            .metadata()
            .get("authorization")
            .and_then(|v| v.to_str().ok())
            .map(|v| v.starts_with("Bearer "))
            .unwrap_or(false);

        if ok {
            Ok(req)
        } else {
            Err(Status::unauthenticated("missing or invalid token"))
        }
    }
}
```

Arrow Flight authentication can be implemented through the Flight handshake, per-call tokens, external negotiation, or gRPC metadata/middleware; the Rust high-level client supports metadata headers for authorization, and tonic provides the server/client TLS and interceptor layers. The Flight spec defines authentication-related error codes `UNAUTHENTICATED` and `UNAUTHORIZED`. ([Apache Arrow][3])

### Auth deployment rules

```text
DO:
  use TLS for all non-local deployments
  prefer bearer/JWT/mTLS/service identity through gRPC metadata
  enforce authz at descriptor/ticket/action level
  avoid putting secrets inside FlightDescriptor or Ticket plaintext
  set deadlines/timeouts
  log request IDs, not tokens

DON'T:
  rely only on client-side SQL filtering for authorization
  expose raw DataFusion catalog without tenant scoping
  return detailed auth failure internals
```

---

## 19.17 DataFusion query server integration

### Architecture

```text
Flight SQL request:
  CommandStatementQuery { query }
  -> SessionContext::sql(query)
  -> DataFrame
  -> execute_stream()
  -> SendableRecordBatchStream
  -> FlightDataEncoderBuilder
  -> DoGet stream

GetFlightInfo:
  validate SQL
  plan query
  derive schema
  allocate query handle / ticket
  return FlightInfo endpoint

DoGet:
  redeem ticket
  execute or resume query
  stream encoded RecordBatches
```

### Query ticket

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct QueryTicket {
    query_id: uuid::Uuid,
}

impl QueryTicket {
    fn encode(&self) -> Ticket {
        Ticket {
            ticket: self.query_id.to_string().into_bytes().into(),
        }
    }

    fn decode(ticket: &Ticket) -> Result<Self, Status> {
        let s = std::str::from_utf8(ticket.ticket.as_ref())
            .map_err(|_| Status::invalid_argument("invalid ticket utf8"))?;
        let query_id = uuid::Uuid::parse_str(s)
            .map_err(|_| Status::invalid_argument("invalid ticket uuid"))?;
        Ok(Self { query_id })
    }
}
```

### DataFusion stream to FlightData

```rust
fn encode_datafusion_stream(
    stream: datafusion_physical_plan::SendableRecordBatchStream,
    schema: SchemaRef,
) -> impl Stream<Item = FlightResult<FlightData>> + Send + 'static {
    let input = stream.map(|batch| {
        batch.map_err(|e| FlightError::ExternalError(Box::new(e)))
    });

    FlightDataEncoderBuilder::new()
        .with_schema(schema)
        .with_max_flight_data_size(2 * 1024 * 1024)
        .build(input)
}
```

### Server rule

```text
GetFlightInfo:
  may plan query and return schema
  should not execute huge query eagerly
  should allocate ticket / query handle with TTL
  should enforce authorization before ticket creation

DoGet:
  executes/polls query
  streams RecordBatch values
  handles cancellation/drop
  frees ticket state on completion/expiry
```

DataFusion execution returns `SendableRecordBatchStream` values, and `FlightDataEncoderBuilder` is designed to encode incremental `RecordBatch` results while preserving stream errors that may occur after earlier batches have already been produced. ([Apache Arrow][5])

---

## 19.18 PyArrow Flight mapping

| PyArrow Flight                             | Rust `arrow-flight`                                  |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `pyarrow.flight.connect(...)`              | `Endpoint::connect()` + `FlightClient::new(channel)` |
| `FlightClient.get_flight_info(descriptor)` | `client.get_flight_info(descriptor).await?`          |
| `FlightClient.do_get(ticket)`              | `client.do_get(ticket).await?`                       |
| `FlightClient.do_put(descriptor, schema)`  | `FlightDataEncoderBuilder` + `client.do_put(...)`    |
| `FlightServerBase` subclass                | implement tonic `FlightService`                      |
| `FlightInfo`                               | `arrow_flight::FlightInfo`                           |
| `FlightEndpoint`                           | `arrow_flight::FlightEndpoint`                       |
| `Ticket`                                   | `arrow_flight::Ticket`                               |
| `Location`                                 | `arrow_flight::Location`                             |
| `FlightStreamReader`                       | `FlightRecordBatchStream`                            |
| auth header                                | `client.add_header(...)` / tonic metadata            |
| TLS options                                | tonic `ClientTlsConfig` / `ServerTlsConfig`          |

Agent caveat:

```text
PyArrow Flight has Python-specific convenience objects.
Rust Flight uses tonic/prost types directly.
Do not search for a one-method clone of every PyArrow Flight call; map to the underlying RPC shape.
```

---

## 19.19 Flight SQL mapping

| Flight SQL intent        | Rust client/server                                                                        |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| execute query            | `FlightSqlServiceClient::execute(...)` / `get_flight_info_statement` + `do_get_statement` |
| execute update           | `execute_update` / `do_put_statement_update`                                              |
| list catalogs            | `get_catalogs()` / `get_flight_info_catalogs`                                             |
| list schemas             | `get_db_schemas` / `get_flight_info_schemas`                                              |
| list tables              | `get_tables(CommandGetTables)` / `get_flight_info_tables`                                 |
| table types              | `get_table_types()` / `get_flight_info_table_types`                                       |
| SQL server info          | `get_sql_info(Vec<SqlInfo>)` / `get_flight_info_sql_info`                                 |
| primary keys             | `get_primary_keys` / `get_flight_info_primary_keys`                                       |
| imported/exported keys   | `get_imported_keys`, `get_exported_keys`                                                  |
| cross reference          | `get_cross_reference`                                                                     |
| prepare statement        | `prepare(query, transaction_id)` / `ActionCreatePreparedStatementRequest`                 |
| bind parameters          | `PreparedStatement::set_parameters(RecordBatch)` / DoPut prepared-statement query/update  |
| close prepared statement | `PreparedStatement::close()` / `ActionClosePreparedStatementRequest`                      |
| transaction begin/end    | Flight SQL actions / server-specific transaction manager                                  |
| ingest                   | `CommandStatementIngest` / DoPut ingest                                                   |

## 19.20 Middleware and observability

### Tower/tonic service layers

```rust
use tower::ServiceBuilder;
use tonic::transport::Server;

let layer = ServiceBuilder::new()
    .timeout(std::time::Duration::from_secs(60))
    .into_inner();

Server::builder()
    .layer(layer)
    .add_service(FlightServiceServer::with_interceptor(service, AuthInterceptor))
    .serve(addr)
    .await?;
```

### Observability fields

```text
Per RPC:
  method
  descriptor type/path/cmd hash
  ticket hash
  query id
  tenant id
  peer address
  auth subject
  batches sent
  rows sent
  bytes sent
  elapsed
  error code
  cancelled flag

Never log:
  raw authorization header
  raw ticket if it contains sensitive state
  raw SQL in high-sensitivity environments without redaction policy
```

## 19.21 Deployment profiles

### Internal Flight data service

```text
Use:
  core FlightService
  DoGet / DoPut / GetFlightInfo
  bearer or mTLS auth
  schema-first GetSchema
  simple Ticket encoding

Avoid:
  Flight SQL unless database-style SQL metadata/prepared statements are required
```

### SQL query service backed by DataFusion

```text
Use:
  Flight SQL
  SessionContext
  GetFlightInfo -> plan/schema/ticket
  DoGet -> execute_stream -> FlightDataEncoderBuilder
  metadata APIs as much as clients require
  PreparedStatement only if client ecosystem needs it

Avoid:
  full transaction claims unless storage/query engine supports them
```

### External client interoperability

```text
Use:
  spec-compliant FlightInfo / Ticket / FlightEndpoint
  Flight SQL metadata schemas
  TLS
  conservative dictionary handling
  small enough gRPC messages
  integration tests with PyArrow, JDBC/ODBC/ADBC clients if claimed
```

---

## 19.22 Performance rules

```text
Do:
  stream RecordBatch values
  set max FlightData size below gRPC max message size
  use execute_stream, not collect, for large DataFusion queries
  bound query concurrency
  use deadlines and cancellation
  use one endpoint if strict ordering is required and client support is uncertain
  pre-project/filter queries before streaming
  avoid tiny batches
  avoid huge batches that exceed gRPC limits
  use compression only after benchmarking

Do not:
  collect query results before DoGet
  encode enormous single FlightData messages
  perform blocking IO in tonic async handlers
  keep prepared statements/tickets forever
  put large query state directly into tickets without size/security review
```

---

## 19.23 Anti-pattern catalog

| Anti-pattern                                   | Failure mode                       | Correct pattern                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `GetFlightInfo` executes full query            | latency/memory blowup              | plan + ticket only                                 |
| `DoGet` returns collected `Vec<RecordBatch>`   | memory blowup                      | stream `SendableRecordBatchStream`                 |
| raw SQL stuffed into ticket                    | sensitive logs / giant tickets     | opaque query id                                    |
| no ticket TTL                                  | leaked query state                 | expiry + cleanup                                   |
| unsupported Flight SQL methods silently wrong  | client incompatibility             | return `UNIMPLEMENTED`                             |
| advertise transactions without backend support | correctness violation              | expose `SqlInfo` accurately                        |
| prepared statement never closed                | leaked server resources            | client close + server TTL                          |
| no TLS in production                           | data/token exposure                | tonic TLS / mTLS                                   |
| authorization only at query text layer         | data leak through metadata/tickets | enforce at RPC, descriptor, ticket, catalog levels |
| logging tokens/tickets                         | credential/state leak              | hash/redact                                        |
| dictionary encoding unchecked                  | interop failures                   | hydrate or test target clients                     |

---

## 19.24 Golden test matrix

```text
Core Flight:
  GetSchema returns correct schema
  GetFlightInfo returns endpoint + ticket
  DoGet streams batches
  DoGet unknown ticket -> NOT_FOUND
  DoPut upload round trip
  DoAction custom action
  ListFlights discovery
  ListActions discovery
  cancellation
  max message size splitting
  dictionary arrays hydrate/resend behavior

Flight SQL:
  execute SELECT
  execute UPDATE affected rows
  get_catalogs
  get_db_schemas
  get_tables
  get_table_types
  get_sql_info
  get_primary_keys
  imported/exported/cross-reference keys
  prepared statement create
  parameter_schema / dataset_schema
  set_parameters
  prepared execute
  prepared execute_update
  close prepared statement
  transaction unsupported -> UNIMPLEMENTED
  transaction supported path if implemented

Security:
  missing auth -> UNAUTHENTICATED
  forbidden table -> PERMISSION_DENIED
  TLS client/server handshake
  mTLS if used
  token expiry
  ticket TTL

Interop:
  Rust client -> Rust server
  PyArrow client -> Rust server
  Rust client -> PyArrow/example server if available
  Flight SQL client compatibility
  dictionary columns
  timestamps/timezones
  decimals
  large strings/binaries
```

---

## 19.25 Value case

```text
Flight RPC:
  value = Arrow-native network transport for RecordBatch streams.

FlightData:
  value = IPC-framed schema/dictionary/batch messages over gRPC.

FlightInfo:
  value = discovery, partitioned endpoints, schemas, size estimates, and fetch coordinates.

Ticket:
  value = opaque server-controlled stream handle.

Location:
  value = same-service, alternate Flight server, or HTTP/HTTPS external resource routing.

FlightDataEncoderBuilder:
  value = convert DataFusion/Arrow RecordBatch streams into gRPC FlightData streams with error propagation.

FlightRecordBatchStream:
  value = decode remote FlightData into Arrow RecordBatch stream.

Flight SQL:
  value = database/client ecosystem protocol over Arrow Flight.

Prepared statements:
  value = parameter binding, server-side planning, SQL client compatibility.

Transactions:
  value = database semantics when backend truly supports them.

Tonic integration:
  value = Rust async server/client, TLS, interceptors, middleware, deadlines.

DataFusion integration:
  value = SQL query engine + Arrow-native network result streaming.
```

Final agent rule:

```text
Use core Flight for Arrow data service APIs.
Use Flight SQL for database-compatible SQL APIs.
Use tonic for server, TLS, auth, middleware, deadlines.
Use FlightDataEncoderBuilder for DoGet.
Use FlightRecordBatchStream for DoGet clients and DoPut servers.
Use DataFusion execute_stream for query result streaming.
Return FlightInfo from planning/discovery.
Redeem Ticket in DoGet.
Treat prepared statements, tickets, and transactions as server resources with TTL, authz, and cleanup.
```

# 20) ADBC and database connectivity

Style target: dense, syntax-first, agent-ready technical reference; aligned with the uploaded advanced-reference format. 

---

## 20.0 Mental model

```text id="ot92pg"
ADBC =
  Arrow Database Connectivity
  vendor-neutral database access API
  SQL + Substrait query execution
  catalog/metadata APIs
  Arrow RecordBatchReader result sets
  Arrow RecordBatch / RecordBatchReader parameter binding and ingestion

Rust ADBC =
  adbc_core             # native Rust trait definitions and shared types
  adbc_datafusion       # native Rust DataFusion driver
  adbc_driver_manager   # FFI driver-manager wrapper for C-compatible ADBC drivers
```

ADBC is Arrow-native database connectivity for SQL/Substrait queries, catalog metadata, and result sets using Arrow data; the Rust ADBC library is a standalone implementation whose primary crate is `adbc_core`. Current `adbc_core` docs list native Rust driver traits `Driver`, `Database`, `Connection`, and `Statement`, and explain that native Rust drivers avoid C FFI overhead. ([arrow.apache.org](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/main/rust/index.html)) ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/adbc_core/latest/adbc_core/))

---

## 20.1 Version and status anchors

```toml id="o6e5ka"
[dependencies]
adbc_core = "0.23.0"
adbc_datafusion = "0.23.0"
adbc_driver_manager = "0.23.0"
```

Current docs.rs latest for `adbc_core`, `adbc_datafusion`, and `adbc_driver_manager` is `0.23.0`; `adbc_datafusion 0.23.0` depends on Arrow `58.1.x` family crates and DataFusion `53.0.x`, so version alignment with the rest of the Arrow/DataFusion stack matters. ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/adbc_core/latest/adbc_core/)) ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/adbc_datafusion/latest/adbc_datafusion/)) ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/adbc_driver_manager/latest/adbc_driver_manager/))

Driver status is not uniform: current ADBC status docs mark the Rust DataFusion driver experimental, while the Flight SQL driver implementation is Go and stable; C-compatible drivers, including Flight SQL, can be used from Rust via the driver manager. ([arrow.apache.org](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/main/driver/status.html)) ([arrow.apache.org](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/main/driver/flight_sql.html))

---

## 20.2 Cargo profiles

### Native DataFusion ADBC driver

```toml id="t5t09z"
[dependencies]
adbc_core = "0.23.0"
adbc_datafusion = "0.23.0"

arrow-array = "58.4.0"
arrow-schema = "58.4.0"

datafusion = "54.1.0"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt-multi-thread", "macros"] }
```

Use when Rust code wants an ADBC-compliant interface over an in-process DataFusion engine.

### Driver manager / dynamic drivers

```toml id="q1tucd"
[dependencies]
adbc_core = "0.23.0"
adbc_driver_manager = "0.23.0"

arrow-array = "58.4.0"

```

Use when loading C-compatible ADBC shared libraries at runtime: SQLite, PostgreSQL, Flight SQL, DuckDB, or vendor drivers.

```toml id="qwyx2z"
[dependencies]
adbc_core = "0.23.0"

arrow-array = "58.4.0"
```

### Version-drift warning

```text id="s3yx42"
If cargo emits multiple Arrow crate versions:
  run cargo tree -d
  align arrow-array / arrow-schema / datafusion / adbc_datafusion
  avoid mixing incompatible Arrow major versions
```

The official Rust ADBC quickstart explicitly warns that mismatched Arrow versions in the dependency graph can produce Rust type errors and recommends using `cargo tree` and controlled `cargo update` operations to converge versions. ([github.com](https://github.com/apache/arrow-adbc/blob/main/docs/source/rust/quickstart.rst?plain=true))
